title: Uddalaka: the thread and the inner controller (3.7)
hook: the salt-and-banyan father of the Chandogya steps up as a challenger, with a question a spirit once asked him
tomorrow: Gargi returns: "two questions, like two arrows"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gargi asked what everything is woven on, all the way to the top, until Yajnavalkya stopped her. Your line was the weave. Did you notice the threads holding each other? Day three hundred seventy-eight.

An old friend steps up. In the Chandogya, Uddalaka Aruni was the father who dropped salt in water and split a banyan seed for his son, and said: you are that. Now he stands up in Janaka's court as a challenger. And like Bhujyu, he brings a question from a spirit. Years ago, he says, a spirit speaking through a woman asked us: do you know the thread that strings this world, the next world and all beings together? Do you know the inner controller? Yajnavalkya, if you drive off those cows without knowing them, your head will fall off.
screen: `THE FATHER FROM THE CHANDOGYA.` → `A SPIRIT'S QUESTION.` → `THE THREAD, AND THE CONTROLLER.`

segments.voice: I know them, Yajnavalkya says. Anyone can say I know, I know, says Uddalaka. Tell us. The thread, says Yajnavalkya, is wind: like a string through beads, it holds this world and the next together. Then the inner controller, in a long chant. He who lives in the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who rules the earth from within: he is your self, the inner controller, the deathless. Then again, the same lines, for water. For fire. For the sky, the wind, the sun, the directions, the moon and stars, space, darkness, light, all beings. Then it turns inward: the breath, speech, the eye, the ear, the mind, the skin, understanding. Over and over: he lives in it, it doesn't know him, it is his body, he rules it from within. And the close. He is the unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, the unknown knower. There is no other seer but him. And Uddalaka falls silent. Later schools built on this passage. Ramanuja, the Vishishtadvaita teacher, took its key phrase, whose body the earth is, and taught that the world and every soul are the body of God, who lives within them as their inner ruler. Shankara, the Advaita teacher, read the inner controller as the one self, appearing as ruler from the side of the world. Look back at this week of the debate. The priest. The name. The razor's edge. The seer. The child. The weave. And today, the one inside it all, unseen.
screen: `ANYONE CAN SAY I KNOW, I KNOW.` · `THE THREAD IS WIND.` · `WHOSE BODY THE EARTH IS.` · `THE UNSEEN SEER.` · then, large: `ANTARYAMIN.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the one within. Sit, and breathe. Feel the breath, and let the line come: lives in the breath, yet other than the breath. Then the eyes, resting: lives in the eye, yet other than the eye. Then the mind, with all its traffic: lives in the mind, yet the mind doesn't know it. You don't have to believe anything. Just notice whether something steady seems to sit under each of these, watching. The bell holds the time.
Uddalaka. The teacher who asked about the thread and the antaryamin, the inner controller: the one who lives in each thing, whom the thing doesn't know, and who rules it from within.
Your line: antaryamin. Today, touch the ground once, a floor or the earth, and remember: whose body the earth is. Day three hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: The antaryamin passage is central in Sri Vaishnava theology, where God is understood as the inner ruler of all; students of other Vedanta schools study it too, and the antaryamin is invoked in devotional hymns.

fork.setup: Uddalaka says: anyone can say I know, I know. you're Yajnavalkya. what do you do?
options: say exactly what the thread and the inner controller are.
fork.reveal: he tells them: the thread is wind; the inner controller lives in everything, unknown by it, ruling it from within. Uddalaka falls silent.

original.note: Sanskrit antaryāmin: antar (within) + yam (to hold, to rule): the one who rules from within.

trapdoor: what you thought: a controller, like someone pulling strings.
what it means: the one who lives in each thing, other than it, unknown by it, its inmost self.
what a scholar hears: the antaryāmi brāhmaṇa (3.7) is a key text for Ramanuja's śarīra-śarīri teaching, the world as God's body; Shankara reads it as the one self.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.12–13 (Uddalaka, the banyan seed and the salt)
Ramanuja, Sri Bhashya (the world as the body of Brahman)

notes: The gandharva (Kabandha Atharvana) and the house of Patanchala Kapya are omitted for listening ease; the spirit spoke through Kapya's wife (3.7.1). Confirm.
Lists in 3.7.3–23 are abbreviated; confirm the selection.
Ramanuja's and Shankara's readings are stated briefly and side by side; confirm fairness. Madhva's reading is not given.
The Uddalaka of BU 3.7 is generally identified with the Chandogya's Uddalaka Aruni; confirm.
